To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Ca2+ spikings in the outer cortex of M. truncatula roots occur in a distinct pattern during infection by both rhizo-bacteria (Rhizobium) and fungi (Glomus) and that these patterns are similar in terms of frequency, suggesting that the Ca2+ spike signature is not specific to the type of microbe that is infecting the host.

1) distinct oscillatory Ca2+ profiles in root cortical cells correlate with specific stages and/or types of endosymbiont infection; 2) Ca2+ spikinig in outer cortical cells is a prerequisite for the reversible formation of pre-infection threads and pre-penetration apatatus; 3) a transition to high-frequency Ca2+ spikiing occurs at the time of initial cell entry by endosymbionts; 4)

(i) distinct Ca(2+ )oscillatory profiles correlate with different stages of transcellularr infection by both rhizia and arbuscular Mycorrhizal Fungi (AMF), (ii) low frequency Ca(2+)spiking in the outer cortex precedes infection, and (iii) a transition from low- frequency to high frequency spiking is concommitant with the initial stagesof apoplastic cell entrance by both microbes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms underlying the symbiotic interactions between legumes and rhizobia and between arbuscular mycorrhyzae and plants.
the role of Ca(2+) in the development of symbiosis.
the role of calcium as a signaling component of the host response to endosymbionts in the legume root.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
calcium signaling is an important part of the signaling cascade in root endosymbiosis, and it is a key player at the stage of cell entry.
Ca(2+) plays an important role in the regulation of endosymbiosis in plants.

the Ca2+ oscillations observed in the outer cortex during the early stage of the infection process are likely to be involved in the regulation of cell wall remodeling, cell division and the establishment of the symbiosis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Ca(2+) is a key player during the commitment of root cells to endosymbiosis, with the spiking signature changing in response to different symbionts and different infection strategies.
Ca(2+) is a key player during endosymbiotic interactions.
Ca(2+) is an early and critical component of the signaling network that controls the commitment to endosmbiotic infection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Ca(2+) signals play a central role during root cell entry of both endosymbiotic bacteria and fungi.

Ca(2+) signatures can be used as a readout for different stages of endosymbiont infection and that these signatures are conserved across different symbioses, indicating that they are likely to be important for the establishment of endosymbiosis.
the Ca(2+)-based signaling pathway that is involved in early recognition of the microbes in the epidermis is also active during subsequent transcellular infection of the cortex by both microbes.
